title: Hurricane Isaias forecast to bring dangerous storm surge, with millions under warnings in US
summary:
Residents in areas from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Florida urged to ‘evacuate if told to do so’

Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida are under hurricane warnings on…

blocks.text: Millions of people from Louisiana to Florida are under hurricane warnings on Thursday as Hurricane Isaias heads toward the US Gulf coast, with weather officials warning of dangerous storm surge, hurricane-force winds, heavy rainfall and flooding.

Isaias intensified from a tropical storm into the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday night, and has prompted state of emergency declarations in Florida and Alabama, as well as evacuation orders and school closures in several Florida counties as officials urge residents to prepare for its arrival.

The National Weather Service (NWS) said on Thursday morning that Isaias, currently a category 1 hurricane with sustained winds of 85mph (137km/h), is expected to pass to the north of the Yucatán peninsula later in the day on Thursday, before reaching the northern Gulf coast, where it is expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday.

The NWS warned that Isaias is “expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday” and that it is expected to bring a “life-threatening storm surge” along parts of the northern Gulf coast.

Storm surge warnings, issued when there is a “danger of life-threatening inundation from rising water moving inland from the coastline”, are already in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwanee River in Florida. Residents in the affected areas have been urged to follow advice from local officials and evacuate if instructed to do so.

Hurricane warnings are in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf county line in Florida, with the NWS warning that “damaging hurricane force-winds are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama, and southern Mississippi”. Residents are being urged to prepare for possible “long-duration power outages”.

Tropical storm warnings are in effect from parts of Louisiana to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and from east of the Bay/Gulf county line to Aucilla River in Florida. Gusty winds are also possible across parts of the Yucatán peninsula on Thursday.

Isaias is expected to bring heavy rain to the central Gulf coast and much of the south-east from Friday into the weekend, with 3-7in of rain expected from south-eastern Louisiana to the Florida Big Bend region. The NWS warned that localized rainfall totals of up to 15in are possible, and noted that flash and urban flooding is possible, along with isolated river flooding.

Isolated tornadoes could also develop Friday night in coastal areas of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle and far south-western Georgia, the NWS said, adding that “the tornado threat will continue Saturday for eastern Alabama, Georgia and northern Florida”.

Alabama governor Kay Ivey declared a state of emergency in 40 counties on Wednesday, saying the order would allow officials to take “any needed steps ahead of landfall”. The declaration remains in effect until 14 October. A flood watch is also set to take effect for all of central Alabama from 7pm local time on Friday through 7am local time Saturday morning.
The Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, also declared a state of emergency this week for 25 counties as the state prepares.

At a news conference on Thursday afternoon, DeSantis said that the hurricane is “expected to make impacts with the winds as early as Friday afternoon” and said that “landfall is projected at this point to be late Friday night into the wee hours of Saturday morning. It’s moving pretty quickly.”

“Execute your plan now if you’re in that area, execute it, it’s something that we’re going to have to get through, we’re going to have impacts, and I’ve pretty much said that from the outset, there will be impacts,” he said, adding: “We are assuming that this could reach category three status.”

At the local level, several counties in Florida have issued local emergencies and evacuation orders. Officials in Okaloosa county declared a local state of emergency on Wednesday and ordered some residents in coastal areas to evacuate.

On Thursday, Florida’s Walton and Franklin counties issued mandatory evacuation orders for some areas. Officials in Escambia county also issued an evacuation order for residents in areas including Perdido Key, Innerarity Point, Pensacola Beach and other low-lying areas.

DeSantis said on Thursday that the Florida division of emergency management was coordinating with all local counties to address resource requests and to position equipment before the storm. He also said that 900 personnel with the Florida department of transportation were conducting pre-storm preparations.
Several school districts in Alabama and Florida have announced closures, while Florida State University’s Tallahassee campus announced it will be closed on Friday.

The hurricane is also expected to disrupt travel. The Federal Aviation Administration warned on Thursday that Isaias may “lead to Gulf route closures” while the Southern Rail Commission said that Amtrak’s Mardi Gras service along the Gulf coast will be suspended through the weekend. Additionally, starting Friday, the Crescent service between New Orleans and Atlanta will be suspended until Monday.

In Tennessee, the NWS office in Morristown warned that “remnants of Hurricane Isaias will bring heavy rain and strong, gusty winds to our area this weekend”. The office said that “high winds could top 60–70+ mph in the eastern TN mountains and foothills, with isolated flash flooding possible in heavy rainfall areas”.

In Ohio, the NWS office in Wilmington cautioned that Isaias will hit the Ohio valley this weekend, with strong winds expected, with possible “widespread rain” and storms. In Pennsylvania, the NWS office in Pittsburgh said that “moisture from Hurricane Isaias is forecast to reach our region this weekend” and that they were expecting “soaking rain, but risks of significant flooding are low”.
